This has now been answered completely, by S. Kutin, L. Smithline and V. Vatter, Permutation Wordle, arXiv:2609.01874 (September 2026). They mention this question in their introduction.

The strategy. Their strategy is CircularShift. Guess the identity first. After each round, keep every entry that was correct, and shift the incorrect values one step to the right, cyclically, among the incorrect positions.

Its performance. CircularShift solves $\sigma$ in exactly $\operatorname{exc}(\sigma)+1$ guesses, where $\operatorname{exc}(\sigma)$ is the number of excedances, the $i$ with $\sigma(i)>i$. So the number of permutations it solves in exactly $k+1$ guesses is the Eulerian number $A(n,k)$, and, for a uniformly random secret, the expected number of guesses is $$E(n)=\frac{n+1}{2}.$$ In the notation of the question, $E(n)\sim cn$ with $c=1/2$.

Optimality, in the strongest sense. Their Theorem 10 says that every deterministic strategy solves at most $\sum_{k\le d}A(n,k)$ permutations within $d+1$ guesses, for every $d$. This holds even when the guesses may be arbitrary words over $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Theorem 11 extends the bound to randomised strategies, so no strategy has smaller expected number of guesses than $(n+1)/2$.

The conjecture first appeared in the earlier paper of Kutin and Smithline (arXiv:2408.00903). A. Hiveley (J. Integer Seq. 29 (2026), Art. 26.1.7) proved it for games of at most three guesses within a class of strategies built from CircularShift.
